name: Aniracetam
lead: Aniracetam is a racetam-family nootropic, a synthetic compound related to piracetam that was developed by Hoffmann-La Roche in the 1970s as Ro 13-5057 [1]. In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a mood, calm and focus aid: people who take it say it lowers social anxiety and sharpens verbal fluency, which they connect to carrying themselves more confidently and expressively.

Pharmacologically it is best known as a positive allosteric modulator of AMPA-type glutamate receptors, slowing the receptors' desensitization and deactivation [2][3]. In some countries it has been used as a prescription medicine for cognitive decline in older adults, and it is sold elsewhere as a supplement or research chemical [1].

Published human work consists mainly of 1980s and 1990s trials in elderly patients with dementia or cerebrovascular disease, plus a review of animal studies that included models of anxiety, depression and attention [4][5][6].

chain: Users report lower social anxiety and better verbal fluency
angle.text: People use aniracetam hoping for calmer, more fluent social interaction, which they feel shows in expression, eye contact and general presence. The link to looks is through confidence and demeanor rather than any physical change.

card.summary: A racetam nootropic that people take for calm focus and easier social fluency, supporting a more confident, expressive presence.
card.note: Not FDA-approved; available mainly as a supplement or research chemical.

quick.overview:
Aniracetam is a nootropic in the racetam family. It is taken for focus, mood and reduced social anxiety, and in looksmaxxing circles it is mentioned as a way to feel and appear more at ease and articulate in social settings.

It began as a Roche research compound in the 1970s and has been used as a prescription drug for cognitive decline in some countries. Elsewhere it is sold as a supplement.
quick.mechanism: It positively modulates AMPA glutamate receptors, prolonging their response to glutamate, and has been reported in animal work to affect acetylcholine, serotonin and dopamine signalling. It is absorbed and metabolized rapidly, with a short half-life.
quick.risks: Trials in older adults reported it was generally tolerated, with mild gastrointestinal effects the most commonly mentioned. In one 1987 trial confusion led to treatment interruption in a few participants. It is not approved by the FDA or EMA, so products are unregulated in many regions.

infobox: Prescription in some countries (e.g. Italy); not FDA/EMA approved [1]

paras: Aniracetam has no direct physical effect on appearance. Users describe it as taking the edge off social anxiety and improving word-finding and mood, and treat it as a way to come across more relaxed and engaged. These accounts are anecdotal [1].

The social-confidence idea rests on aniracetam's reputation as an anxiolytic-like nootropic. Rodent work reviewed in 2002 covered models of fear, anxiety and depression as well as attention and arousal [6], and Wikipedia notes a 2001 mouse study reporting anxiolytic-like effects [15]. Forum users typically describe the hoped-for payoff in everyday terms: easier small talk, less hesitation before speaking, and a more animated face and voice. Those descriptions are self-reports; no controlled study has measured them in healthy adults.
It has been used in some European countries for behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia and for cognitive problems after stroke or in Alzheimer's disease [6].

Aniracetam enhances AMPA receptor currents by reducing desensitization and slowing deactivation, an effect described in electrophysiology studies from 1990 onward [2][7][8]. Reviews of racetams also describe interactions with cholinergic systems [9].

Within the wider racetam family, piracetam-type nootropics have been studied for decades without a single agreed mechanism, and aniracetam is the member most closely tied to AMPA-receptor modulation [16]. Studies of how positive allosteric modulators act on AMPA receptors examine how compounds such as aniracetam change receptor deactivation and desensitization [19]. Rodent studies also describe effects on acetylcholine release, and a 2024 review proposed that aniracetam might influence amyloid processing through BDNF and metabotropic glutamate receptor pathways, a hypothesis that remains at the preclinical level [9][17].

After a 200 mg oral dose, its main metabolites, anisic acid and p-methoxyhippuric acid, peaked at about 2 hours in elderly patients with cerebrovascular disease and returned to baseline by about 6 hours [10].

Wikipedia gives the elimination half-life as roughly half an hour, because oral aniracetam undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism in the liver; the main metabolites are N-anisoyl-GABA, 2-pyrrolidinone and p-anisic acid, and N-anisoyl-GABA may account for part of the acetylcholine-releasing effect seen in rats [15]. Its anisoyl group makes it more lipophilic than piracetam, which Grokipedia says helps it cross the blood-brain barrier [1].

Hoffmann-La Roche synthesised aniracetam in the 1970s, with related patents published in 1979 [15]. Rodent experiments from 1982 onward reported better learning and memory in animals whose function had been impaired, for example by scopolamine or electroconvulsive shock, which led to its being grouped with the nootropics [15][18]. Human trials followed through the 1980s and early 1990s in dementia and cerebrovascular disease [4][5][11].

Outside clinics, interest grew in the 2000s as online nootropics communities swapped reports on racetams, and aniracetam became one of the better-known options alongside piracetam and phenylpiracetam [1].

A double-blind trial randomized 44 patients with Alzheimer-type dementia to aniracetam 1 g daily or placebo for three months; confusion interrupted treatment in four aniracetam and one placebo participant [4]. A placebo-controlled multicentre study in senile dementia and a trial in elderly people with mental deterioration were also published [5][11]. An intravenous study used a human hypoxia model [12]. A registered 2026 study is examining IQ-test reliability under modafinil and racetam-class compounds in healthy adults [13]. In pigeons, aniracetam did not improve working memory [14]. No published trial has tested it for social confidence in healthy adults.

The 1987 double-blind trial reported that treatment was interrupted by confusion in four aniracetam and one placebo participant, and its authors examined neurological and psychometric measures over three months [4]. The 1991 multicentre study in senile dementia of the Alzheimer type, which used the Roche code Ro 13-5057, is the larger of the two controlled trials [5]. A 1997 pharmacokinetic study compared elderly patients with cerebrovascular disease to young healthy volunteers after a single 200 mg dose [10]. The 1984 hypoxia-model study used intravenous aniracetam to look at neurophysiological and psychometric measures in healthy volunteers, the closest published human work to a non-patient population [12]. Studies in healthy adults for social confidence or anxiety are absent from the published literature.

From the 2000s aniracetam spread from medical use into nootropics communities, where users reported focus, mood and creativity effects [1]. In appearance-oriented spaces it appears in 'stack' discussions about social fluency and calm, usually next to caffeine and L-theanine or other racetams, with users describing effects as subtle and short-lived. These accounts are anecdotal.

Legal status varies. Wikipedia lists prescription availability in Greece (Memodrin, Referan) and Italy (Ampamet), Schedule 4 prescription-only status in Australia since the February 2020 Poisons Standard, and, in the United States, treatment as an unapproved new drug that is nonetheless found in dietary supplements sold online [15]. Brand names include Draganon, Sarpul, Ampamet, Memodrin and Referan [15].

Trials in older patients described aniracetam as generally well tolerated; mild gastrointestinal complaints are most often mentioned, and the 1987 trial recorded confusion leading to treatment interruption in a few participants [1][4]. Long-term safety in healthy adults, and the quality of unregulated supplement products, have not been studied in published trials.
